abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: To improve the energy density of LiFePO4 (LFP) cathode materials for Li-ion cells, we have utilized a modified mechanofusion method for preparing micrometer-sized LFP/C composite flake particles. The resulting flake particle morphology resulted in improved packing efficiency, enabling an electrode porosity of 14% to be achieved at high loadings, which represents a volumetric energy density increase of 28% compared to conventional LFP. Furthermore, LFP/C flake composites electrodes were found to have a higher coulombic efficiency, a reduced voltage–polarization, and a greatly reduced charge transfer resistance compared to conventional LFP electrodes. This is believed to be due to the low surface area of the LFP/C flake composite particles coupled to fast Li+ ion grain boundary diffusion. The ability to make highly dense LFP and low surface area electrodes could have profound impacts, allowing for Li-ion cells to be made with low cost and low environmental impact LFP, while high achieving volumetric energy densities and high coulombic efficiencies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Li-ion batteries (LIBs) have high gravimetric and volumetric energy density and moderate cost, making them the most widely used secondary battery chemistry in consumer electronics, electric vehicles (EVs), and grid storage applications.1 However, the mass application of LIBs, especially in the latter two applications, requires reductions in cost and environmental impact and improved sustainability.1,2 The cathode materials used in LIBs contribute significantly to these factors. This is because the majority of Li-ion batteries utilize layered LiMO2 oxide cathode materials, where M = Co (LCO), a mixture of Ni, Mn, and Co (NMC), or a mixture of Ni, Co, and Al (NCA). All these cathode materials utilize Co, which is relatively high in cost and low in earth abundance. The common coprecipitation synthesis route for the mixed metal layered oxides is also high in cost, uses large volumes of water, and is energy intensive.

A promising alternative cathode material, LiFePO4 (LFP), introduced by Padhi et al. in 1997, has attracted significant attention.3 The advantage of using LFP compared to the layered oxides is that iron is naturally abundant, making LFP lower in cost and environmentally friendly.4 In addition, LFP has a high thermal stability and excellent cycle life. However, compared to layered oxide cathode materials, LFP has poor electronic conductivity and low Li+ ion diffusion kinetics.5−8 To improve the overall performance of LFP, particle size reduction and carbon coating is generally used to reduce Li+ diffusion lengths and improve electronic conductivity.9−12 However, reducing particle size results in amplified electrolyte reactivity due to increased surface area. In addition, volumetric capacity is also affected by size reduction, which results in poor packing efficiency and low cathode active loadings. For instance, typical LFP coatings used in energy applications have porosities of about 25–30% and active loadings of about 18 to about 21 mg/cm2,13 corresponding to ∼1.7–2.0 mAh/cm2 for a 60 μm thick coating. In comparison, typical layered oxide coatings for energy applications have porosities less than about 25% and active loadings in excess of 4 mAh/cm2. A chief barrier for achieving greater LFP active loadings is its poor packing efficiency, which results in coating fracture and delamination if higher loadings or higher calender densities are attempted. As a result of these limitations, LFP has limited use in applications requiring high energy densities.

Various methods to increase LFP electrode energy density have been described previously. These include spray-dried LFP/carbon composites,14 utilizing particle distributions,15 and isostatic pressing under very high pressures.16 In all cases, the LFP or LFP/carbon composites utilized were composed of submicrometer particles or had high surface area, which may be detrimental toward electrolyte reactivity. Most studies also utilize very low (∼1 mAh/cm2) electrode loadings. All of these studies report that high density LFP electrodes can have lower impedance than conventional LFP electrodes made from submicrometer LFP particles.

In this study, we explore the use of large (i.e., ∼5 μm) and fully dense LFP particles as an alternate means to achieve high energy density LFP electrodes. High density electrodes with good mechanical properties are commercially made on a large scale from conventional layered cathode materials in the form of fully dense 5–10 μm particles. Therefore, if fully dense 5–10 μm LFP particles could be made, then high electrode densities should also be practically achievable with conventional electrode coating/calendering processes. Utilizing large and dense LFP particles should also result in a low surface area and increased coulombic efficiency. The problem to solve with this approach then reduces to making large and dense LFP particles with good electrochemical properties. However, it is not immediately apparent if this is even possible, considering the low Li+ diffusion kinetics and poor electrical conductivity of LFP.

One clue that making large and dense LFP particles with good electrochemical properties could be achievable comes from the above-mentioned studies of high-density calendered LFP coatings.16 As mentioned above, these studies report that high-density LFP electrodes can have lower impedance than conventional LFP electrodes made from submicrometer LFP particles. The densified electrode coatings made in these studies can be considered as highly dense LFP/carbon composite monoliths. Although such monoliths also contain a small amount of porosity and polymeric binder, their good electrochemical behavior does give a suggestion that large particle LFP/carbon composites might function as practical electrode materials. Such particles could be made, for instance, by grinding highly densified LFP/carbon coatings. However, this method would likely not be a scalable process. Furthermore, the resulting particles would contain binder and some porosity, which would lower their energy density.

What is required is a process to make highly dense LFP/carbon composite particles with no binder and very little carbon content. For practical use, the particles should be at least 5 μm in size and have a low surface area (i.e., smooth surfaces with low porosity). Ideally the particles should be made up of submicrometer or nanometer LFP grains surrounded by carbon to reduce bulk Li+ diffusion lengths and improve electrical conductivity. Recently we developed a method of granulating nanoparticles and nanoparticle mixtures into compact large particles called dry particle microgranulation (DPMG).17 In this process a mixture of submicrometer or nanosized feedstock particles and larger (∼50 μm) spherical template particles is mechanofusion processed. The transformation of the feedstock particles during this processing can be considered to occur in two stages. Initially, the template particles are coated with a highly densified layer of feedstock particles. This first stage of the process occurs rapidly (within minutes). If mechanofusion processing is continued, then in a second stage, the feedstock coating eventually spalls off and spheronizes. As a result of the entire DPMG process, the feedstock particles are transformed from submicrometer or nanosized particles into monodisperse and fully dense ∼10 μm compact particles (i.e., they are microgranulated). However, the DPMG process can be lengthy (e.g., 20+ h).17 This is mainly due to the length of time required for the feedstock particle coating to spall off the template particles and spheronize in the second stage of the process.

In this study, we show that the DPMG method can be modified, so that the first and second stages of the process are separated and accomplished via two different methods. This results in a reduction in the processing time from >20 h to minutes. Furthermore, particles made according to this modified process have a flake morphology, which results in high powder packing densities. Because of the resulting flake morphology, we have called this new method “dry particle flaking” (DPF). Applying DPF to submicrometer LFP–graphite feedstock powder mixtures, we show that fully dense and low surface area ∼10–15 μm LFP/C composite particles with a flake morphology can be produced. Graphite was chosen as a carbon source because it is likely to exfoliate and form highly conductive graphene in the high-shear fields produced during mechanofusion processing. We further show that highly densified electrodes can be made from such particles by conventional calendering that have exceptional energy density and improved lithium diffusion kinetics compared to conventional LFP electrodes.

sec.title: Synthesis of Dense LFP/Carbon Flake Composite Particles
sec.p: Mixtures of conventional carbon-coated LiFePO4 (LFP) (P198-S13, BTR New Materials Groups Co. Ltd., China) and natural graphite (Grade 230U, Asbury Graphite Mills, Kittanning, PA) in different weight ratios according to Table 1 were mechanofusion processed with 225 g template particles (50 μm ZrO2 spheres, Glen Mills) (total powder volume ∼50 mL) using a modified AM-15F Mechanofusion System (Hosokawa Micron Corporation, Osaka, Japan). The mechanofusion parts were modified by replacing the stainless-steel bowl, press head, and scraper with identical parts made from hardened steel. Mechanofusion processing was performed for 30 min at a speed of 1500 rpm with a 1.4 mm press-head gap and a 0.5 mm scraper gap. This resulted in the formation of an LFP/carbon coating layer on the surface of the template particles. About 80 g of the LFP/carbon-coated template particles was then impact milled using an impact grinder (CBG110S/Black+Decker) by pulse grinding (∼1 s/pulse) for 15–20 pulses, resulting in the formation of a mixture of LFP/carbon composite flake particles and template particles. The LFP/carbon composite flakes were separated from the mixture using a 38 μm sieve. The recovered LFP/carbon composite flake particulate was then heated in a flowing 95% Ar and 5% H2 gas mixture at a temperature of 650 °C for 10 h. The final LFP/carbon composite flakes are referred to here as F-LFP#, where # refers to the weight percent carbon in the flake, according to Table 1.

sec.title: Sample Characterization
sec.p: X-ray diffraction patterns were measured using a Rigaku Ultima IV diffractometer equipped with a Cu Kα X-ray source, a diffracted beam monochromator, and a scintillation detector. Each XRD pattern was collected from 10° to 80° 2θ with 0.05° increments for 3 s per step. Sample morphology was examined using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) (JSM-IT200 InTouchScope, JEOL Ltd.) with 10–15 kV accelerating voltage. Electrodes were cross-sectioned for SEM imaging using an argon ion beam in a cross-section polisher (IB-19530 CP, JEOL Ltd.). SEM images of single-particle cross sections were obtained by the Canadian Centre for Electron Microscopy (CCEM) (Hamilton, Ontario, Canada) using a focused ion beam (FIB) paired with high-resolution SEM (Helios 5 UC DualBeam, Thermo Scientific). Specific surface areas were determined by the single-point Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) method with N2 gas using a surface area and pore size analyzer (Nova 4200e, Quantachrome Instruments). True densities were determined using helium pycnometry (AccuPyc II 1340, Micrometrics).

sec.title: Electrode Preparation
sec.p: Electrode slurries consisted of sample material, carbon black (Super C65, Imerys Graphite and Carbon), and poly(vinylidene fluoride) binder (PVDF, Sigma-Aldrich) in a 93:4:3 weight ratio. An appropriate amount of 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.5% anhydrous) was added to achieve a proper coating viscosity. Slurries were mixed for 30 min using a high-shear mixer and then spread onto aluminum foil with a 0.006 in. (0.15 mm) gap coating bar and dried in air for 90 min at 120 °C. The resulting electrodes had an average active loading of 4.8 mg/cm2.

LFP and F-LFP2 electrodes were additionally prepared with higher active loadings of 12–15 mg/cm2. Such high active loading electrodes had a 90:5:5 active:carbon black:binder weight ratio and were prepared using the same procedure as stated above, except their slurries were spread onto aluminum foil with a 0.016 in. (0.41 mm) gap coating bar. Selected high active loading electrodes were calendered with a 6 in. constant gap calender (DPM Solutions, Hebbville, NS). All electrodes were cut into 1.3 cm diameter disks and heated under a vacuum overnight at 120 °C prior to cell assembly. Electrode porosities were determined based on the coating weight, the known true densities of the electrode components, and the coating thickness (measured to within ±1 μm with a Mitutoyo 293-340 precision micrometer), according to the method described in ref (18).

sec.title: Electrochemical Cell Preparation, Assembly, and Testing
sec.p: Cell assembly was performed in an Ar-filled glovebox. Sample electrodes were assembled in 2325-type coin cells with a copper spacer, a lithium foil (99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) counter/reference electrode, a polypropylene/polyethylene/polypropylene trilayer separator (Celgard 2300, Celgard, LLC, Charlotte, NC), a polypropylene blown microfiber (BMF) membrane (3M Company), the sample electrode, and an aluminum spacer. 1 M LiPF6 (Gotion Inc.) in a solution of ethylene carbonate (EC, Soul Brain), diethyl carbonate (DEC, Soul Brain), and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC, BASF) (volume ratio 3:6:1) was used as electrolyte. Cells were cycled galvanostatically at 30.0 ± 0.1 °C between 2.5 and 3.65 V with the first (formation) cycle performed at a 0.05C rate and subsequent cycles at a 0.1C rate, where the C rate was based on an LFP capacity of 170 mAh/g. To test rate capability, cells were cycled at a constant 0.1C charge rate with the discharge rate increasing every five cycles from 0.1C to 0.2C, 0.5C, 1C, 2C, 5C, and 10C. All cells were tested using a Maccor Series 4000 Automated Test System (Maccor Inc., Tulsa, OK). For electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements, half-cells were assembled similarly and underwent a formation cycle at 0.05C followed by a 0.1C charge to 60% SOC by capacity. The working electrodes were then harvested from these cells in an argon-filled glovebox and assembled into symmetric coin cells. EIS measurements were carried out on the symmetric cells using a Biologic SP300 potentiostat with a frequency range between 100 kHz and 10 MHz.

sec.title: Dry Particle Flaking Method
sec.p: The dry particle flaking (DPF) method is illustrated schematically in Figure 1. DPF consists of three primary steps. In the first step, a mixture of feedstock particles and hard, smooth, and spherical template particles is mechanofusion processed. The feedstock particles are typically much smaller (e.g., <0.5 μm) than the template particles (∼50 μm). However, feedstock particle size reduction typically occurs during mechanofusion with the template particles. Therefore, if larger feedstock particles are used, they become reduced in size during the initial stages of the mechanofusion step. As mechanofusion proceeds, the feedstock particles form a dense coating on the template particles. The coating of small particles onto large particles is a well-known property of mechanofusion. This process typically occurs within minutes.

caption.p: Schematic diagram of the DPF process.

sec.p: In the second step of the DPF process, the coated template particles are subjected to impact milling. This causes the feedstock particle coating to break off the template particles, as dense flakes ∼10 μm in breadth. This step occurs within seconds. In the third step, the flakes are then separated from the template particles by a classification process. As an overall result of the DPF process, submicrometer feedstock particles are transformed into dense ∼10 μm flakes within minutes. We have further found that the template particles may be reused without washing. Therefore, DPF produces little/no waste.

sec.title: LFP/C Flake Composite Synthesis
sec.p: The DPF process was utilized to make LFP/C composite flakes. Figure 2 shows SEM images that were taken during each step in the process to show how the flake morphology is achieved. The feedstock particles for the process were mixtures of commercially obtained carbon-coated LFP and graphite. The LFP (Figure 2a) consisted of primary particles that are mostly 0.1–1 μm in size. Some of these primary particles are aggregated into secondary particles approximately 5–7 μm in size. Figure 2b shows an SEM image of the graphite feedstock particles, which consisted of a mixture of 5–20 μm flakes and potato-shaped particles. ZrO2 spheres were used as template particles. An SEM image of the ZrO2 template particles is shown in Figure 2c. They consist of smooth and monodisperse spheres that are 50 μm in size.

caption.p: SEM images of (a) LFP starting material, (b) graphite feedstock particles, (c) 50 μm ZrO2 template particles, (d) coated LFP/C template particles following mechanofusion, (e) coated LFP/C template particles and free composite flakes following impact milling, (f) unheated LFP/C composite flakes, and (g) heated LFP/C composite flakes.

sec.p: In the first step of DPF processing, LFP–graphite particle mixtures were mechanofusion processed with the template particles. Within 30 min of mechanofusion processing, all of the feedstock particles formed a dense LFP/C composite coating on the spherical template particles, as shown in Figure 2d. Any carbon coating that was on the surface of the LFP particles would now be incorporated in the particles in an amount that is typically used for carbon coating LFP (∼0.5–2 wt %).19 As will be shown below, carbon from the original carbon coating on the LFP particles and the 5–20 μm particle graphite added to the mechanofusion process were transformed during mechanofusion to disordered carbon that is too small to detect by SEM. The LFP/C-coated template particles were then impact milled, which resulted in much of the LFP/C composite coating breaking off the template particles in the form of flakes, as shown in Figure 2e. The flakes were then separated from the template particles by sieving. An SEM image of the resulting LFP/C carbon composite flake particulate is shown in Figure 2f. These particles were then heated to improve the crystallinity of the LFP. During this heating step, the flake morphology was maintained, as shown in Figure 2g.

Figure 3a–d shows SEM images of LFP and F-LFP with 0%, 2%, and 5% graphite content, respectively. Pristine LFP particles are primarily 0.1–1 μm in size, with aggregates that are 5–7 μm. In contrast, all F-LFP compositions have an increased particle size compared to LFP, while having a characteristic flake morphology, with the individual particles having a width of about 10–15 μm and a thickness of about 2 μm.

caption.p: SEM images of (a) LFP, (b) F-LFP0, (c) F-LFP2, and (d) F-LFP5.

sec.p: The particle sizes, surface areas, densities, and particle porosities of the LFP and F-LFP samples are given in Table 2. Particle porosities were calculated from the measured densities by assuming that each particle was made up of its solid constituents (with densities equal to their bulk densities) and empty pore spaces. Consistent with its increased particle size, there is a significant reduction (∼50%) in surface area of the F-LFP0 and F-LFP2 samples compared to LFP. This may be beneficial as a low surface area is generally associated with improved CE due to reduced parasitic reactions with the electrolyte. Using helium pycnometry, the particle density of F-LFP0 and F-LFP2 was only slightly less than LFP. Taking into account the bulk density of their constituents, this corresponds to a particle porosity (i.e., the closed pores that cannot be accessed by He(g)) of only 1.3% for F-LFP0 and only 1.1% for F-LFP2. This implies that the F-LFP0 and F-LFP2 flakes are highly densified with almost no internal void space. In contrast, F-LFP5 had a 4-fold increase in surface area compared to F-LFP0 and F-LFP2. This increase in surface area was concurrent with an almost 4-fold increase in particle porosity. These results suggest that the F-LFP5 particles are not dense, but instead have an open structure, leading to a high surface area. This was verified by SEM images, as will be discussed further below. These results show that if excessive graphite is added to LFP in the DPF process in amounts greater than 2%, then particles with an open porous structure result. Therefore, to achieve highly densified F-LFP particles with low surface area, it is vital that the graphite content be kept low (<5%).

fn.p: Here, the average particle size was determined from the SEM images. Because of the preferred orientation of the flake particles in the images, this average size reflects the size of the basal planes of the flake particles.

sec.p: Figure 4a–c shows XRD patterns of the initial LFP–graphite feedstock powder mixture, the product of the DPF process, and the final F-LFP particles after postheating, respectively, for the case of F-LFP2 synthesis. The inset in each panel of Figure 4 shows an expanded view of the graphite (002) peak. Figure 4a shows the XRD pattern of the feedstock LFP–graphite particle mixture. The XRD pattern of the LFP component of this mixture is characteristic of highly crystalline LFP having an ordered olivine structure indexed to the orthorhombic Pnma space group. The graphite component of the mixture is characteristic of a highly graphitized carbon. Figure 4b shows the XRD pattern of this sample after DPF processing. All the characteristic LFP peaks are still evident; however, they are broader and have reduced intensity, which indicates a reduction in grain size and the formation of defects. The relative LFP peak ratios have also changed after DPF processing. In particular, the intensity of the (101) peak (near 21°) has increased in relation to the other peaks. As will be shown below, this is consistent with a preferred LFP crystallite orientation in the [101] direction. In the case of the graphite phase, only the (002) peak (near 27°) is evident in the XRD pattern. The peak shape has not changed compared to the (002) peak of the graphite in the unprocessed feedstock powder; however, the (002) peak intensity is reduced. The reduction in the intensity of the LFP and graphite phases after DPF processing may be caused by the amorphization of a portion of these phases during the DPF process. This is supported by the broad peak in the XRD pattern of the DPF processed LFP–graphite mixture that extends from about 19°–40°, which is indicative of the presence of an amorphous phase. This peak can be more easily seen in Figure S1, which shows the same XRD patterns with the intensity plotted on a log scale. The broad peak of the DPF processed LFP–graphite mixture is centered in the region with the highest intensity graphite and LFP peaks, suggesting that it is due to either amorphous carbon, amorphous LFP, or both.

caption.p: XRD patterns of (a) a hand-mixed LFP–graphite mixture used as a control sample, (b) F-LFP2 flake composite materials following DPF processing, and (c) F-LFP2 flake composite materials after heating.

sec.p: Postheating was applied to the DPF processed samples to increase their crystallinity. Figure 4c shows the XRD pattern of the F-LFP2 sample after postheating. The XRD peaks of the F-LFP2 sample become narrower, and any evidence of the material being partially amorphized is removed. However, the relative peak intensity ratios in F-LFP2 are significantly different from those of the LFP starting material. Rietveld refinements of the XRD patterns were used to quantify the observed changes. Details of the refinements are described in the Supporting Information, and refinement results are listed in Tables S1 and S2. No significant changes in lattice constants, atom positions, or occupancies between LFP and F-LFP2 could be detected in the refinements. Instead, good refinements for the F-LFP2 XRD pattern were obtained when the preferred orientation according to the March–Dollase model was included with the preferred orientation in the [101] direction. This resulted in a March coefficient of 0.93, which suggests the crystallites are plate-like in shape with the [101] direction normal to the plates and the plates orientated parallel to the diffraction plane.20 In other words, the grains making up the F-LFP2 particles are plate-like, with their (101) planes in preferential alignment with the basal planes of the flake particles. This result is in contrast with the LFP sample, which showed no preferred orientation.

The formation of the plate-like LFP crystallites described above in the F-LFP2 sample suggests that the LFP grains preferentially fracture along their (101) planes as a result of shear forces during the mechanofusion process. That the LFP grains would fracture in this way is consistent with studies that show that strain is minimized in LFP grains if phase boundaries lie along the LFP (101) direction.21 The alignment of the LFP grains such that they are configured in a layered manner parallel to the flake particle basal plane was verified in SEM images. This is discussed below in relation to Figure 5. With regard to the graphite phase in the F-LFP2 composite particles, an expanded view of the graphite (002) peak is shown in the inset of Figure 4c. This peak is much lower in intensity because of the heating process, indicating that some graphite has been lost during this process. This could be caused, for example, by the reaction of graphite with any oxygen impurities that might exist in the furnace atmosphere.

caption.p: Particle cross sections of a single F-LFP2 particle utilizing a focused gallium-ion beam (FIB) showing (a) a top-down view of a particle etched by an FIB directed at the top of the particle and (b) a view perpendicular to the basal plane of a particle that was cross-sectioned by a FIB.

sec.p: XRD patterns of LFP and all of the F-LFP samples are shown in Figure S2, and Rietveld refinement results are listed in Tables S1 and S2. No significant variation in lattice constants, atom positions, or site occupancies could be detected among the samples. Similar to the F-LFP2 sample, the F-LFP0 sample exhibited a strong preferred orientation parameter of 0.904 in the [101] direction. However, the F-LFP5 sample showed significantly less preferred orientation (Pk = 0.969). These results suggest that, like the F-LFP2 sample, the F-LFP0 sample experienced significant shear stress during DPF processing, resulting in the formation of flake-like LFP grains. However, the LFP grains in the F-LFP5 sample apparently experienced less shear stress, resulting in less preferred orientation. These results are confirmed by SEM images and will be discussed below in relation to the images shown in Figures 5 , Figure S4, and S5.

Williamson–Hall plots (shown in Figure S3) were constructed from the XRD patterns of LFP and F-LFP samples to determine their grain size and lattice strain. Here grain size refers to the size of the single crystal grains that make up each particle, whereas particle size refers to the external size of the particles observed using SEM. Only peaks with widths greater than the diffractometer’s experimental broadening were included in the analysis. From this analysis, the LFP sample was found to have an average grain size of 289 nm and a lattice strain of 0.04%. The grain size and lattice strain of the LFP phase in the F-LFP2 sample were determined to be 161 nm and 0.05%, respectively. F-LFP0 and F-LFP5 also show reductions in grain size (206 and 180 nm, respectively) while a slight increase in lattice strain is observed for F-LFP0 (0.08%) and F-LFP5 (0.05%). Therefore, DPF processing followed by heating resulted in reductions in grain size and slight increases lattice strain compared to the LFP starting material. The observed grain size reduction is believed to contribute to the improved rate performance of F-LFP compared to LFP, as will be shown below.

Figure 5 shows SEM images of single F-LFP2 particles that have been sectioned by utilizing a focused gallium-ion beam (FIB). In Figure 5a the F-LFP2 flake is oriented such that its surface is roughly parallel to the plane of the page. Etching this flake by FIB from above revealed internal layering, with the layers being parallel to the flake basal plane. Figure 5b shows an FIB cross section that is perpendicular to the flake basal plane.

Much of the particle is solid; however, some closed pores are visible. The amount of closed pore volume visible in Figure 5b is substantially greater than the 1.1% closed void space predicted from helium pycnometry measurements. Many of the closed pores are extremely small (∼50 nm) nanovoids and are surrounded by a light border in the secondary electron image. The composition of these lighter shaded regions could not be determined because the particle composition appeared homogeneous within the spatial resolution of the EDS detector. However, especially near the top of the image, these lighter shaded regions predominantly occur on the outside surfaces of individual grains. Considering that the graphite in these samples would reside in a separate phase outside of the LFP grains, which is coincident with the location of these pores, we speculate that these small voids are formed by the vaporization of carbon in the sample during the FIB etching process. Void formation due to sample vaporization is a well-known artifact of ion beam polishing.22 These voids being formed during the ion milling process would also explain why the amount of closed pore volume observed in Figure 5b is greater than the 1.1% closed void space predicted from helium pycnometry measurements.

Interestingly, the arrangement of nanovoids in Figure 5b is not random but rather is such that suggests a lamellar structure. Obvious lines of nanovoids running through the structure in this image are highlighted in Figure S4. We suggest that this microstructure can be attributed to the DPF process, where the template particles are coated with LFP and graphite particles, while this coating is simultaneously subjected to high shear forces, which causes the shearing and smoothing of the graphite and LFP particles along the template particle surface (as has been previously observed during mechanofusion processing of polycrystalline NMC).23 If, as suggested from the XRD results, the LFP predominately shears along the (101) planes in this process, then such a mechanism would result in sequential layers of graphite and LFP crystallites oriented parallel to the flake basal plane. During subsequent heating, the LFP particles would crystallize, causing grain growth and partial disruption of the layered structure. This grain growth is apparent on the top of the image shown in Figure 5b. During the grain growth, the LFP grains apparently maintain a preferred orientation with the (101) planes parallel to the flake basal plane. This layered structure would explain the layered appearance of the FIB section shown in Figure 5a, which would result from differences in the erosion rates of graphite and LFP layers.

SEM images of argon broad-ion-beam (BIB) cross sections of electrode coatings made with LFP, F-LFP0, F-LFP2, and F-LFP5 are shown in Figure S5a–d, respectively. Because these images are of electrode coatings, carbon black and binder are visible between the larger LFP and F-LFP particles. As shown in Figure S5a, the LFP particles are dense with no internal porosity. The F-LFP0 particles have a small internal porosity and appear to have been formed from small grains of LFP that have been fused together. This fusing process is likely due to high shear and compressive forces experienced during DPF processing, which results in the preferred orientation of the LFP grains, as observed in the F-LFP0 XRD pattern. Figure S5c shows the BIB cross section of a F-LFP2 electrode. As with the FIB cross section, tiny white nanovoids can be observed, which are thought to be due to the vaporization of graphite by the argon-ion beam. However, in BIB cross-sectioning, the layering of the nanovoids is not obvious. This may be due to the disturbance of the sample by the much coarser argon-ion beam than the fine gallium beam used for FIB. Similar to the F-LFP0 sample, the F-LFP2 sample is almost completely dense and only contains a small amount of nanovoids. The extreme shear and compressive forces that must have been responsible for fusing the individual LFP grains into these dense particles is also consistent with the preferred orientation of the LFP grains in the F-LFP2 sample, as observed by XRD. In contrast to the F-LFP0 and F-LFP2 samples, the F-LFP5 sample is not dense but contains a high degree of porosity. The higher graphite content in the sample has apparently inhibited the LFP grains from fusing, so that this sample consists of submicrometer LFP particles that have only been partially fused together. This lack of particle fusing is consistent with a lack of distortion of the particles, resulting in a less preferred orientation observed in the F-LFP5 sample XRD pattern. The open structure of the F-LFP5 particles is also consistent with the high surface area observed for this sample.

sec.title: Electrochemistry of LFP/C Composite Flake Particles
sec.p: Figure 6a shows the first cycle potential profiles of LFP and of F-LFP with 0%–5% graphite content. The potential profile of the LFP sample is typical of battery-grade LFP. It has a single plateau at about 3.3 V with a 163 mAh/g reversible capacity, an almost negligible irreversible capacity, and a low voltage polarization of about 90 mV. In comparison, F-LFP0 has a low reversible capacity (146 mAh/g), a high irreversible capacity (9.1 mAh/g), and a higher voltage polarization. This is not surprising, considering the poor electrical conductivity and lithium-ion diffusion of LFP. Therefore, the greatly increased size of the F-LFP particles compared to the conventional LFP sample would be expected to result in increased lithium diffusion path lengths, an increased particle electrical resistance, and a reduction in the number of surface sites for lithium intercalation.

caption.p: Galvanostatic cycling results of LFP and F-LFP flake composites with varying graphite content. (a)Voltage–capacity profiles. (b) Reversible capacity and CE. (c) Polarization versus cycle number.

sec.p: With the addition of graphite, improved electrochemical performance is observed for the F-LFP samples. Adding 2 wt % graphite results in the F-LFP2 sample achieving a reversible capacity of 159 mAh/g, a nearly negligible irreversible capacity, and a voltage polarization of 80 mV. Except for a slightly lower capacity, this performance exceeds that of the pristine LFP sample. To achieve this improvement in performance compared to F-LFP0 and LFP, the graphite in the F-LFP2 sample must serve to both increase electrical conductivity and facilitate fast Li-ion diffusion in the grain boundaries. The slightly lower capacity of the F-LFP2 sample compared to LFP is consistent with the amount of inactive graphite present in the composite structure. To verify this, F-LFP5 was synthesized. As shown in Figure 6a, F-LFP5 has similar characteristics as F-LFP2, except that its reversible capacity is lower (154 mAh/g). As shown in Figure S6, most of the capacity reduction in the F-LFP2 and F-LFP5 samples can be attributed to the presence of inactive graphite.

Figure 6b shows the discharge capacity and CE vs cycle number of LFP and F-LFP with 0%–5% graphite content. LFP retained 98.2% of its capacity over 50 cycles. In contrast, F-LFP0 retained only 89.56% of its capacity over 9 cycles, when cycling was stopped due to excessive capacity fade. This fade is consistent with the known performance of large particle size LFP that has not been carbon coated due to LFP’s low electronic conductivity and low Li+ ionic conductivity.24 Furthermore, the average CE for F-LFP0 over 9 cycles is 96.9% in comparison to LFP, which had an average CE of 99.8% over 50 cycles. The low average CE of F-LFP0 is due to the capacity fade observed, indicating a loss of active material through increased polarization or complete electrical disconnection. The addition of graphite to form F-LFP/C composites led to significant improvements in capacity retention and CE. The addition of 2% graphite led to a capacity retention of 99.3% and an average CE of 99.90% over 50 cycles, which is superior to the performance of pristine LFP. To achieve this performance, the addition of graphite must improve both electronic and ionic conductivity. It is well-known that carbon addition (e.g., by carbon coating) improves the electronic conductivity of LFP. It is less clear why the ionic conductivity should improve. However, for good lithiation kinetics to occur in such large LFP particles, the graphite addition must be enabling fast Li+ diffusion along grain boundaries. Similar cycle life was observed for F-LFP5, indicating that addition of graphite beyond 2 wt % does not improve performance further. However, the CE of F-LFP5 was reduced compared with that of F-LFP2, which can be attributed to its higher surface area. The higher CE achieved by F-LFP2 compared to LFP is attributed to its reduced surface area, resulting in decreased electrolyte reactivity and thus reducing lithium inventory loss.

Figure 6c shows the polarization of LFP and of F-LFP with 0–5% graphite content. LFP has an initial polarization of about 80 mV, which then continuously increases with cycling to a value of 130 mV. This polarization increase may be reflective of the relativity high reactivity of LFP with electrolyte due to its large surface area. In contrast to LFP, all of the F-LFP samples show an initial decrease in polarization during cycling. The number of cycles over which this decrease in polarization occurs seems to increase with the amount of graphite in the F-LFP. Because highly calendered LFP electrodes also show an initial decrease in cell polarization during cycling (as will be shown below), we suspect that this could be an electrolyte wetting effect.

The F-LFP0 electrode had the highest polarization, which is expected on account of the poor electronic conductivity of large particles of nearly pure LFP with no carbon coating. The cell polarizations observed for F-LFP2 and F-LFP5 are almost identical and are much lower (∼70 mV after 50 cycles) than that of LFP (∼130 mV after 50 cycles). This is astonishing, considering that it is commonly believed that to achieve low polarization with LFP requires submicrometer particle sizes and carbon coating.24,25 In the case of F-LFP, much lower polarization than a conventional LFP sample was obtained with large particles and with no carbon coating. The similar polarization of the F-LFP2 and F-LFP5 cells indicates that increasing graphite beyond 2 wt % does not significantly reduce impedance. Therefore, the F-LFP2 composition was selected for more detailed studies.

Figure 7 shows the discharge capacity of LFP, F-LFP2, and F-LFP5 cells cycled at different rates. Initially, the capacities of F-LFP2 and F-LFP5 are lower than those of LFP to a degree greater than can be accounted for just by the inactive graphite in their compositions. However, in accordance with its observed initial decrease in impedance during cycling, the F-LFP2 capacity increases to its expected capacity by cycle 10. As the cycling rate increases, the capacity of LFP drops at a faster rate than does F-LFP2 or F-LFP5, indicating that F-LFP2 and F-LFP5 have superior rate capability in comparison to LFP. At a 1C rate, F-LFP2 matched the capacity of LFP, whereas the capacity of F-LFP5 was slightly lower. As the discharge rate was increased to 2C, 5C, and 10C, the capacity of F-LFP2 and F-LFP5 greatly exceeded that of LFP. At 10C, LFP had almost negligible discharge capacity, while F-LFP2 and F-LFP5 retained about 65% of their initial capacity. At the end of the rate test, the cells were allowed to continue to cycle at a C/10 rate. The LFP cell had a slightly lower capacity than it did initially, while the F-LFP2 and F-LFP5 capacities increased. This is consistent with the continuously increasing polarization of LFP and decreasing polarization of F-LFP2 and F-LFP5 during cycling.

caption.p: Rate capability of LFP, F-LFP2, and F-LFP5 uncalendered electrodes at varying rates.

sec.p: Figure 8 shows Nyquist EIS plots of LFP, F-LFP2, and F-LFP5 symmetric cells. In this figure, the impedance was normalized by multiplying the measured impedance by the average active mass. The impedance represented by the diameter of the semicircle, denoted here as Rtotal, is associated with a combination of the charge transfer resistance, the contact resistance between the current collector and electrode material, and the ionic resistance of the SEI layer. F-LFP2 has a significantly smaller Rtotal (0.09 Ω·g) compared to that of LFP (0.43 Ω·g). This represents a 4-fold reduction in impedance. Similarly, F-LFP5 has a significantly smaller Rtotal (0.12 Ω·g) compared to LFP representing close to a 4-fold reduction in impedance. However, the impedance observed is higher than F-LFP2. For further analysis, EIS data were fitted using the equivalent circuit shown in Figure 8 with the calculated equivalent circuit parameters shown in Table S3. A depressed semicircle observed in the high frequency range was attributed to Li+ migration resistance through the cathode interface formed on the electrode, a second semicircle in a mid-frequency range was assigned to the diffusion of Li+ in grain boundaries within the LFP particles, and a third semicircle corresponds to diffusion at very low frequencies, which, combined with a Warburg impedance element, was associated with bulk Li-ion diffusion within LFP grains. Bulk Li+ diffusion coefficients (DLi+) were calculated from the Warburg coefficients. It was determined that LFP, F-LFP2, and F-LFP5 had diffusion coefficients of 2.7 × 10–11, 9.3 × 10–11, and 3.0 × 10–11 cm2 s–1, respectively. The slight improvement in the bulk diffusion kinetics of F-LFP2 compared to LFP is consistent with its lower LiFePO4 grain size, which would result in a reduced probability to encounter defects along Li+ conducting channels.25 However, F-LFP5, with similar grain size to F-LFP2 has almost identical bulk diffusion coefficient as LFP. Therefore, the reason for improved bulk diffusion in F-LFP2 may be additionally due to the flake morphology of the grains and their preferred orientation with the F-LFP2 particles, as observed by XRD. The only slight improvement in bulk diffusion kinetics also further confirms that the observed improved kinetics of the F-LFP2 electrode in cycling tests is primarily due to fast Li+ diffusion in grain boundaries. As far as can be determined from SEM and XRD results, the grain boundaries of F-LFP2 seem to be composed of graphitic and amorphous carbon sandwiched between layers of LFP. Why Li+ diffusion should be fast in such grain boundaries is not known.

caption.p: Nyquist plots of symmetric cells with LFP, F-LFP2, and F-LFP5 uncalendered electrodes. The plots were fit by using the equivalent circuit shown.

sec.title: Evaluation of LFP/C Flake Composite Calendered Electrodes
sec.p: Commercial LFP electrodes are typically calendared to the lowest porosity achievable without coating delamination. In practice, this corresponds to an LFP active mass density of about 1.8–2.1 g/mL in the electrode coating.13 To achieve such densities in this study, a high electrode loading of about 14 mg/cm2 was targeted, and electrodes were calendered to the highest degree possible before delamination. To achieve the highest electrode densities and volumetric capacities possible with the highest rate and CE, F-LFP2 was utilized because it exceeded the other F-LFP samples in all of these attributes. Table 3 lists the achieved loading, coating density, active density, and porosity for calendered LFP and F-LFP2 electrodes. Here the calendered electrodes are denoted as LFP[31P] and F-LFP2[14P], where the numbers in the square brackets indicate the minimum porosity achieved prior to delamination. A high electrode density that compares well with those of typical commercial coatings was achieved for the LFP[31P] electrode. This corresponds to a coating porosity of 31%. In contrast, a much greater (25% increase) coating density could be achieved with the F-LFP2[14] electrode. This represents a coating porosity of only 14% and an active material density that exceeds that of commercial LFP electrodes.

caption.title: Summary of Calendered LFP and F-LFP2 Electrode Characteristicsa

fn.label: a
fn.p: Here the active density refers to the amount of active material per unit volume in the coating.

sec.p: The ability of F-LFP2 electrodes to achieve much greater coating densities than LFP is revealed in the SEM images of cross sections of LFP[31P] and F-LFP[14P] electrodes. Figure 9a shows an SEM image of a cross section of the LFP[31P] electrode. This electrode comprises randomly packed submicrometer LFP particles and some larger LFP secondary particles separated by empty pores, binder, and carbon black. There is poor packing efficiency due to the irregular LFP particle shape and random particle arrangement, which is consistent with the inability of this electrode to achieve a high coating density. Figure 9b shows an SEM image of a cross section of the F-LFP[14P] electrode. This electrode also contains the active particles separated by porosity, carbon black, and binder. However, the F-LFP[14P] flake particles have preferentially aligned parallel with the current collector, resulting in a greatly improved packing efficiency compared with LFP[31P] and a higher coating density.

caption.p: Electrode cross sections of (a) LFP[31P] electrode and (b) F-LFP2[14P] electrode.

sec.p: Figure 10a shows the voltage curves of the F-LFP2[14P] and LFP[31P] electrodes. The LFP electrode had an initial coulombic efficieny (ICE) of 98.7% and a reversible capacity of 161 mAh/g. In contrast, the F-LFP2 electrode had much improved ICE of 99.6% and a similar reversible capacity of 162 mAh/g. Figure 10b shows the capacity and CE vs cycle number, and Figure 10c shows the polarization vs cycle number for these electrodes. In both cases, the polarization of these electrodes initially decreases, and the capacity initially increases during cycling, which may indicate that electrolyte wetting is improving over these cycles. The maximum capacities achieved by these electrodes is 160.83 mAh/g for LFP[31P] and 161.64 mAh/g for F-LFP2[14P]. This corresponds to energy densities of 1180 Wh/L for LFP[31P] and 1513 Wh/L for F-LFP2[14P], representing an energy density increase of ∼28% for F-LFP2[14P] compared to LFP[31P]. In addition to a much higher energy density, the F-LFP2[14P] electrode has an improved capacity retention, a greater average CE (99.9% vs 99.4%) and a lower polarization (90 mV vs 130 mV at cycle 50). These improved characteristics can be attributed to the faster Li+ diffusion kinetics of F-LFP2 that results in low polarization coupled with its reduced surface area that leads to reduced parasitic side reactions with the electrolyte.

caption.p: (a) Voltage–capacity profiles of calendered LFP[31P] and F-LFP2[14P] electrodes. (b) Reversible capacity and CE. (c) Polarization with respect to cycle number of calendered LFP[31P] and F-LFP2[14P] electrodes.

sec.p: EIS measurements were conducted on the F-LFP2[14P] and LFP[31P] electrodes shown in Figure 11. A value of Rtotal of 0.07 Ω·g was obtained for the F-LFP2[14P] electrode, which is much smaller compared to the Rtotal value of 0.23 Ω·g observed for the LFP[31P] electrode. This is a 4-fold reduction in impedance, which is similar to that observed for uncalendered electrodes. However, the impedance values of the calendered electrodes are lower. This is consistent with earlier studies of dense LFP electrodes in which impedance was found to be reduced by densification due to improved particle–particle contact and better wetting properties with the electrolyte.15 Therefore, the flake-LFP particles described here may enable highly densified electrodes with improved energy densities compared to conventional LFP, while additionally improving electrode kinetics. Additional improvements may be possible, for instance, by using different sources of carbon (e.g., carbon nanotubes), which may reduce the required carbon content and/or increase rate performance further.

caption.p: Nyquist plots of symmetric cells with LFP[14P] and F-LFP2[31P calendered electrodes.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: A simple and fast all-dry synthesis method was developed for making ∼10 μm sized dense particles from submicrometer particle feedstocks. The resulting particles have a flake morphology. This process was utilized to make LFP/C composite particles from LFP–graphite powder mixtures. Poor electrochemical performance resulted if no carbon was included in the composite. If 2% graphitic carbon was included, then flake particles with a unique microstructure consisting of ∼160 nm LFP grains arranged in layers parallel to the flake basal plane with carbon dispersed between the LFP layers. In this structure, the LFP grains were plate-like and had a [101] preferred orientation direction with respect to the basal plane of the flake particles. The LFP/C composite flake particles also had a surface area of 5.23 m2/g, which was less than half of that of a typical conventional LFP sample (11.69 m2/g).

In lithium cells, it was found that the LFP/C composite had a significantly lower charge transfer resistance compared to conventional LFP, suggesting fast Li+ grain boundary diffusion. The LFP/C composite also attained a higher CE due to reduced surface area. In calendered electrodes, the LFP/C flake composite showed a 28% improvement in energy density compared to a conventional LFP electrode, while showing improvements in cycle life, CE, and polarization. These improvements are thought to be due to a reduced surface area, resulting in reduced electrolyte decomposition reactions, the addition of graphite corresponding to improved conductivity, improved Li diffusion due to fast grain boundary diffusion within the flakes, and improved packing efficiency, which resulted in higher energy density. The high energy density achieved (28% improvement compared to conventional LFP) could have profound impacts on Li-ion cells because it could enable higher energy density and longer cycle life Li-ion cells made with low cost and low environmental impact LFP.
